extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys, patent agents), Office of Enrollment and Discipline staff, and others subject to USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and enumerates the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct and related procedural rules governing suspended/excluded practitioners, reinstatement, client-practitioner duties, conflicts, confidentiality, fees, and other ethical obligations for practice before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to update correspondence address (suspended/excluded/practitioner in disability inactive status)
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded or suspended practitioner, or a practitioner transferred to disability inactive status, shall continue to file a statement in accordance with § 11.11 regarding any change of residence or other address to which communications may thereafter be directed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited recognition for winding up practice (suspended/excluded/practitioner in disability inactive status)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise ordered by the USPTO Director, an excluded or suspended practitioner, or practitioner transferred to disability inactive status, shall not engage in any practice before the Office. The USPTO Director may grant such a practitioner limited recognition for a period of no more than 30 days to conclude work on behalf of a client on any matters pending before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If work cannot be concluded within the limited period, the practitioner must advise the client so the client may make other arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping by excluded/suspended practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded or suspended practitioner, or practitioner transferred to disability inactive status, shall retain copies of all notices sent and maintain records of the various steps taken under this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practitioner shall provide proof of compliance as a condition precedent to the granting of any petition for reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aiding another practitioner while suspended/excluded; acting as a paralegal — conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded or suspended practitioner, or practitioner in disability inactive status, may act as a paralegal for a supervising practitioner or perform other services normally performed by laypersons, provided the conditions in paragraph (h) are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions include: (1) practitioner is under direct supervision of supervising practitioner; (2) practitioner is a salaried employee of the supervising practitioner, the supervising practitioner's law firm, or a client-employer who employs the supervising practitioner as a salaried employee; (3) supervising practitioner assumes full professional responsibility to any client and the Office for any work performed by the practitioner; and (4) the practitioner does not (i) communicate directly with a client or prospective client regarding any immediate or prospective business before the Office, (ii) render any legal advice or legal services regarding any immediate or prospective business before the Office, or (iii) meet in person with specified persons (Office employee concerning prosecution, any client/prospective client regarding business before the Office, or any witness or potential witness) regardless of the presence of the supervising practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement after acting as paralegal while suspended/excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: When an excluded or suspended practitioner acts as a paralegal or performs services under the paralegal conditions, the practitioner shall not thereafter be reinstated to practice before the Office unless specified filings and proofs are made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements include: (i) the practitioner must file with the OED Director an affidavit explaining in detail the precise nature of all paralegal or other services performed and showing by clear and convincing evidence compliance with the provisions and USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct; (ii) the supervising practitioner must file a written statement attesting that they have read the affidavit, believe its statements true, and believe the excluded/suspended practitioner complied with paragraph (h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice of discipline and dissemination of disciplinary information
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall inform the public of the disposition of each matter in which public discipline has been imposed, and of any other changes in a practitioner’s registration status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public discipline includes exclusion, exclusion on consent, suspension, and public reprimand. Unless otherwise ordered, notice of discipline and reasons shall be given to disciplinary enforcement agencies in the State of admission, to courts where the practitioner is admitted, and the public. Final decisions of the USPTO Director shall be published; private reprimands shall result in redacted versions being published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Records of disciplinary proceedings available to the public (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the USPTO Director orders confidentiality, the OED Director’s records of every disciplinary proceeding where a practitioner is reprimanded, suspended, or excluded shall be made available to the public upon written request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information may be withheld to protect third-party privacy or under a protective order. The record of a proceeding resulting in transfer to disability inactive status shall not be available to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to records of exclusion by consent and affidavit use limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: An order excluding a practitioner on consent under § 11.27 and the affidavit required under paragraph (a) of § 11.27 shall be available to the public unless confidentiality is ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information may be withheld to protect third-party privacy or under protective order. The affidavit required under § 11.27(a) shall not be used in any other proceeding except by order of the USPTO Director or upon written consent of the practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on practice until reinstated
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded or suspended practitioner shall not resume the practice of patent, trademark, or other non-patent matters before the Office until reinstated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility timing for petitioning for reinstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded or suspended practitioner shall be eligible to petition for reinstatement only upon expiration of the period of suspension or exclusion and full compliance with § 11.58. An excluded practitioner shall be eligible to petition no earlier than five years from the effective date of the exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement petition filing, fee and threshold review
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for reinstatement must be filed with the OED Director and accompanied by the fee required by § 1.21(a)(10). If the petition is insufficient or defective on its face, the OED Director may dismiss it; otherwise the OED Director shall consider the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standards for proving fitness for reinstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: The excluded or suspended practitioner seeking reinstatement has the burden of proving, by clear and convincing evidence, that: (1) the practitioner has the good moral character and reputation, competency, and learning in law required under § 11.7 for admission; (2) resumption will not be detrimental to the administration of justice or subversive to the public interest; and (3) the practitioner has complied with § 11.58 for the required period (full period if suspended, at least five continuous years if excluded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions on reinstatement — payment of disciplinary costs
rubrics_metrics.description: If reinstatement is granted, it shall be conditioned on payment of the costs of the disciplinary proceeding as set forth in the rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs include: (i) actual expenses for original and copies of reporter's transcripts and reporter fees; (ii) all expenses that would qualify as taxable costs recoverable in civil proceedings; and (iii) charges determined by the OED Director to be 'reasonable costs' of investigation, hearing, and review (excluding fees for attorneys and experts). Relief from assessed costs (including extension of time) may be granted only for hardship, special circumstances, or other good cause at the OED Director's discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of reinstatement — procedural protections and remedial requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If found unfit to resume practice, the OED Director shall provide the petitioner an opportunity to show cause in writing why the petition should not be denied; if unpersuaded, the petition is denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OED Director may require the petitioner to pass the registration examination, attend ethics/substance abuse/practice management courses, and/or pass the MPRE. An aggrieved practitioner may seek review by the USPTO Director under § 11.2(d). Resubmission after denial generally requires waiting at least one year unless the denial order provides otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement proceedings open to public and notice of intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings on any petition for reinstatement shall be open to the public. Before reinstating any practitioner, the OED Director shall publish notice that the practitioner seeks reinstatement and permit a reasonable opportunity for public comment or evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner may, up to 90 days before expiration of suspension/exclusion, file notice of intent to seek reinstatement and request publication; otherwise notice will be published upon receipt of the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence — competence requirement for representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation to a client. Competent representation requires knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence may include legal, scientific, and technical knowledge where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of representation and allocation of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall abide by a client’s decisions concerning the objectives of the representation and, as required by § 11.104, shall consult with the client as to the means by which they are to be pursued. A practitioner may take such action as is impliedly authorized to carry out the representation and shall abide by a client’s decision whether to settle a matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner may limit the scope of representation if the limitation is reasonable and the client gives informed consent. A practitioner shall not counsel or assist a client in conduct the practitioner knows is criminal or fraudulent, but may discuss legal consequences and counsel a good-faith effort to determine validity/scope/meaning/application of the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence — promptness and reasonable diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication — duties to keep and inform client
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall: (1) promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance requiring the client’s informed consent under the Rules; (2) reasonably consult with the client about means to accomplish objectives; (3) keep the client reasonably informed about status; (4) promptly comply with reasonable requests for information; and (5) consult with the client about relevant limitations when the client expects assistance not permitted by the Rules or law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees — prohibition on unreasonable fees and factors for reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not make an agreement for, charge, or collect an unreasonable fee or an unreasonable amount for expenses. Factors to consider in determining reasonableness include: (1) time and labor required, novelty and difficulty, and skill requisite; (2) likelihood acceptance will preclude other employment; (3) customary fee in locality; (4) amount involved and results obtained; (5) time limitations imposed by client or circumstances; (6) nature and length of professional relationship; (7) experience, reputation, and ability of practitioner(s); and (8) whether fee is fixed or contingent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scope of representation and basis or rate of fee/expenses should be communicated to the client, preferably in writing, before or within a reasonable time after commencing representation; changes must also be communicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingent fee requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A contingent fee may be used except where prohibited by law. A contingent fee agreement must be in writing signed by the client and state the method by which the fee is determined, including percentage(s) for settlement/trial/appeal; expenses to be deducted and whether before or after calculation; and must notify client of any expenses for which the client will be liable regardless of outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon conclusion of a contingent fee matter, the practitioner shall provide the client a written statement stating the outcome and, if there is a recovery, showing remittance to the client and the method of its determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of fees between practitioners in different firms
rubrics_metrics.description: A division of a fee between practitioners who are not in the same firm may be made only if: (1) division is in proportion to the services performed or each assumes joint responsibility; (2) the client agrees to the arrangement and share each practitioner will receive and agreement is confirmed in writing; and (3) the total fee is reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of information — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not reveal information relating to the representation of a client unless the client gives informed consent, the disclosure is impliedly authorized to carry out the representation, the disclosure is permitted by paragraph (b), or the disclosure is required by paragraph (c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted disclosures of client information (exceptions to confidentiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may reveal information to the extent reasonably believes necessary: (1) to prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm; (2) to prevent client from engaging in inequitable conduct before the Office or committing crime/fraud reasonably certain to result in substantial injury to another and in furtherance of which the client has used or is using the practitioner's services; (3) to prevent, mitigate, or rectify substantial injury to another resulting from client's crime/fraud in which client used practitioner's services; (5) to establish a claim or defense on behalf of the practitioner in controversy with the client or to respond to allegations in any proceeding concerning the practitioner's representation; (6) to comply with law or court order; (7) to detect and resolve conflicts of interest arising from change of employment or firm composition, but only if privilege not compromised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These permitted disclosures are limited to what the practitioner reasonably believes necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose to the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall disclose to the Office information necessary to comply with applicable duty of disclosure provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable efforts to prevent inadvertent/unauthorized disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall make reasonable efforts to prevent the inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of, or unauthorized access to, information relating to the representation of a client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest — concurrent conflicts (current clients)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not represent a client if the representation involves a concurrent conflict of interest. A concurrent conflict exists if: (1) the representation of one client will be directly adverse to another client; or (2) there is a significant risk that the representation of one or more clients will be materially limited by responsibilities to another client, a former client or third person or by a personal interest of the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notwithstanding a concurrent conflict, representation may be undertaken if (1) practitioner reasonably believes able to provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client; (2) representation not prohibited by law; (3) representation does not involve assertion of claims between clients in same litigation or tribunal; and (4) each affected client gives informed consent confirmed in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific conflict rules — business transactions, gifts, media rights, financial assistance, third-party payments, aggregate settlements, liability limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not enter into a business transaction with a client or acquire an ownership/pecuniary interest adverse to a client unless (1) terms are fair and reasonable and fully disclosed in writing; (2) client is advised in writing of desirability of independent counsel and given reasonable opportunity to seek it; and (3) client gives informed consent in a writing signed by the client. Additional rules: not use information to client's disadvantage absent informed consent; not solicit substantial gifts; not make literary/media rights agreements pre-conclusion; limited exceptions for advancing costs/expenses; not accept third-party compensation without client consent and protection of client information; no aggregate settlements without informed written consent with disclosure; cannot prospectively limit malpractice liability without independent counsel; practitioner shall not acquire proprietary interest in cause of action except permitted liens, contingent fee contracts, and interest in patent/application as part of fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While practitioners are associated in a firm, prohibitions applying to one apply to all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties to former clients
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who formerly represented a client shall not thereafter represent another person in the same or a substantially related matter materially adverse to the former client unless the former client gives informed consent confirmed in writing. A practitioner shall not knowingly represent a person in the same or substantially related matter in which a former firm had represented a client and the practitioner acquired material protected information, unless former client gives written informed consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner shall not use information relating to prior representation to the disadvantage of the former client or reveal such information except as permitted by the Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imputation of conflicts of interest — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: While practitioners are associated in a firm, none shall knowingly represent a client when any one of them practicing alone would be prohibited from doing so by §§ 11.107 or 11.109, unless exceptions apply (personal interest basis or screening with no fee and written notice to affected former client).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a practitioner terminates association, the firm may later represent a person with materially adverse interests unless the matter is the same or substantially related and practitioners remaining have material protected information. Disqualification may be waived by affected client under § 11.107. Disqualification of practitioners associated with former/current Federal Government lawyers governed by § 11.111.

rubrics_metrics.name: Former or current Federal Government employees — compliance with federal ethics law
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who is a former or current Federal Government employee shall not engage in any conduct contrary to applicable Federal ethics law, including conflict of interest statutes and regulations of the department, agency or commission formerly or currently employing said practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Former judge, arbitrator, mediator or other third‑party neutral — representation and employment negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as stated, a practitioner shall not represent anyone in a matter in which the practitioner participated personally and substantially as a judge, law clerk, arbitrator, mediator or other third-party neutral, unless all parties give informed consent confirmed in writing. A practitioner shall not negotiate for employment with any person involved as a party or practitioner in a matter in which the practitioner is participating personally and substantially; a law clerk may negotiate after notifying the judge/official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disqualified, no practitioner in the firm may knowingly undertake the matter unless the disqualified practitioner is timely screened with no fee and written notice is given to parties/tribunal. An arbitrator selected as a partisan on a multimember panel is not prohibited from subsequently representing that party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization as client — who is client and duties when organizational constituents act improperly
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner employed or retained by an organization represents the organization acting through its duly authorized constituents. If the practitioner knows an officer/employee is engaged in or intends action related to representation that is a violation of legal obligation or law likely to result in substantial injury to the organization, the practitioner shall proceed as reasonably necessary in the best interest of the organization, including referring the matter to higher authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If highest authority insists on or fails to address a clearly illegal action likely to result in substantial injury, the practitioner may reveal information relating to the representation to the extent reasonably necessary to prevent substantial injury, even if §11.106 would not otherwise permit disclosure. Paragraph (c) does not apply to information relating to representation to investigate or to defend against alleged violations. Practitioner discharged or who withdraws under related circumstances must take steps to inform organization's highest authority. Practitioner must explain identity of client when organization's interests are adverse to constituents. Practitioner may also represent constituents subject to conflict rules; if organization's consent is required it must be given by an appropriate official other than the individual to be represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client with diminished capacity — preservation and protective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a client’s capacity to make adequately considered decisions is diminished, the practitioner shall, as far as reasonably possible, maintain a normal client-practitioner relationship. If practitioner reasonably believes the client has diminished capacity, is at risk of substantial harm unless action is taken, and cannot adequately act in the client's own interest, the practitioner may take reasonably necessary protective action, including consulting with those who can protect the client or seeking appointment of a guardian or conservator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information relating to such representation remains protected under §11.106, but when taking protective action practitioner is impliedly authorized to reveal information to the extent reasonably necessary to protect the client's interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safekeeping property — separation of client/third-party property and trust account requirement (start)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall hold property of clients or third persons that is in a practitioner’s possession in connection with a representation separate from the practitioner’s own property. Funds shall be kept in a separate account maintained in the state where the practitioner’s office is situated, or else where with the consent of the client or third person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further rules (not fully visible on this page) govern specifics of safekeeping, accounting and disbursement.
